Below is an evidence-backed synthesis of how key process parameters in directed energy deposition (DED) of nickel-based alloys govern deposit geometry, including layer cross-section (width/height/penetration), surface and crown/bridge morphology, and dimensional fidelity. Mechanisms and quantitative trends are highlighted, with alloy-specific notes for nickel-based superalloys such as Inconel 625/718.

1) How DED Forms Deposit Geometry and Why Parameters Matter
- In powder-feed DED, a moving heat source (laser or electron beam) simultaneously melts fed powder and bonds molten material to the substrate and prior layers; geometry emerges from the melt pool’s heat, flow, and solidification under constraints set by toolpath, standoff, and nozzle physics. <cite id="fc17a94e-0">Key controllable inputs include laser/e-beam power, travel speed, powder feed rate, standoff distance, and pass overlap; these directly set clad width, height, penetration depth, dilution, and thus part geometry and microstructural homogeneity</cite>. 
- Alloy chemistry modulates the thermal-transport window; even within “nickel-based,” thermal properties differ enough to shift melt pool dimensions for comparable parameters. <cite id="c53cfda6-2">Inconel 718 shows larger melt pool dimensions than Inconel 625 under similar conditions due to differences in thermal properties, underscoring the need to co-optimize process parameters with alloy-specific thermal behavior</cite>.

2) Power, Speed, and Energy Density: Width, Penetration, and Height
- Laser power is typically the dominant driver of lateral and volumetric geometry: higher power enlarges the melt pool footprint and increases deposition rate, which enlarges clad width and depth and raises material catchment per track. <cite id="fc17a94e-3">In DED of NiTi, laser power critically determines melt pool width and deposition rate; scan speed and feed rate had comparatively smaller effects on cladding geometry across tested ranges, with fluid velocity controlling elemental redistribution within the pool</cite>. <cite id="85e47abf-2">Analytical and experimental studies with coaxial nozzles conclude bead geometry is highly affected by scan speed and laser power, with process maps tying porosity, bead geometry, deposition rate, and powder efficiency to power–speed settings</cite>. 
- Travel speed sets energy density per unit area and time; lowering speed at fixed power increases heat input, deepens penetration, and broadens width, but risks interlayer balling and thermal stress. <cite id="fc17a94e-1">For thin-walled Inconel 738, crack-free deposition was achieved using low scanning speeds to induce high energy density, illustrating how higher energy density enlarges molten pools and stabilizes melting in crack-sensitive nickel-based alloys</cite>. <cite id="c53cfda6-2">Across Inconel 625 and 718, numerical melt pool simulations show material thermal properties govern depth/width; higher effective energy density (low speed/high power) enlarges pools, and alloy differences produce distinct geometry responses at identical parameters</cite>.
- Interaction maps are essential to avoid geometry defects: <cite id="fc17a94e-0">process maps linking power–speed interactions to clad width consistency and porosity below 1% are used to define stable windows; outside these windows, molten pool instability (e.g., balling) degrades geometry and homogeneity</cite>. <cite id="fc17a94e-3">Modeling/experiment correlation shows power governs cladding width and deposition rate, while speed alters residence time and fluid flow, changing cross-section and element distribution</cite>.

3) Powder Feed Rate and Nozzle/Standoff Geometry
- Feed rate sets cross-sectional area per track; it interacts with speed and pool depth to set bead height and surface continuity. <cite id="fc17a94e-0">Industrial DED practice tunes feed rate to target layer heights of 0.5–2 mm, with overlap chosen to fill inter-track gaps and achieve desired cross-section</cite>. <cite id="85e47abf-4">Regression models for bead geometry show bead height, width, and contact angle are functions of laser power, feed rate, powder mass flow, and substrate temperature, enabling prediction of parameters to hit target geometry</cite>. 
- Standoff distance (nozzle-to-workpiece) and laser defocus reshape the beam spot and powder catchment, strongly affecting clad height and width. <cite id="85e47abf-3">For a nickel-based superalloy with a coaxial nozzle, increasing standoff distance first reduces clad width via spot-size and powder distribution changes, then increases clad height at an optimum standoff where powder focuses on the melt pool center, before decreasing height again as powder spreads inefficiently; penetration depth decreases with increased standoff/defocus due to lower energy density and poorer convergence of powder into the pool</cite>. 
- Nozzle physics and powder delivery strategy matter at high rates or off-normal orientations. <cite id="85e47abf-2">Coaxial nozzles concentrate powder into the beam; their efficiency drops on inclined builds due to gravity-driven radial spreading, while discrete coaxial or powder-beam nozzles improve catchment; studies report bead geometry highly sensitive to power/speed in coaxial configurations</cite>. <cite id="85e47abf-2">Zhong et al. showed process parameters control porosity, bead geometry, and powder efficiency simultaneously, reinforcing the need to co-optimize feed, power, and speed for robust geometry</cite>.

4) Cross-Sectional Features: Width, Height, Contact Angle, Dilution, Penetration
- Clad width and height (layer thickness) are the primary descriptors of cross-section; contact angle and dilution quantify bonding and lateral mixing. <cite id="85e47abf-3">Experiments show clad width grows with spot size on the deposition plane; standoff/defocus shift powder distribution and thus width, height, and dilution</cite>. <cite id="85e47abf-4">Design-of-experiments on 1.4404 stainless steel yielded regression models predicting bead height, width, and contact angle from power, feed, powder mass flow, and substrate temperature; models were less reliable for dilution, indicating dilution is sensitive to transient pool behavior and interpass heat</cite>. 
- Penetration depth and dilution evolve with energy input and standoff: <cite id="85e47abf-3">higher energy density and focused powder delivery increase penetration; increasing standoff and defocus reduce spot concentration and lower penetration, while also altering clad height via powder catchment efficiency</cite>. <cite id="fc17a94e-2">In stable deposition beyond the first layer, uniform interfacial microstructures emerge, but dilution effects are strongest at the initial layers where substrate melting and mixing dominate geometry</cite>.
- Alloy-dependent thermal response shapes achievable cross-sections. <cite id="c53cfda6-2">Inconel 718 shows larger melt pools than Inconel 625 at similar parameters; this guides parameter offsets when transferring build geometries between nickel-based alloys</cite>. <cite id="fc17a94e-3">For NiTi, power-dominated width and deposition rate set the cross-section baseline even as speed/feed modulate flow and element distribution; this mechanism generalizes to nickel-based alloys where phase transformation and latent heat can alter pool dynamics</cite>.

5) Surface Morphology, Crown/Bridge Morphology, and Layer-by-Layer Geometry
- Crown height and bridge morphology arise from overlapping beads and molten material redistribution; they are sensitive to energy density, overlap, and standoff. <cite id="fc17a94e-3">High-speed photography of Inconel 718 DED shows accumulation of molten material at protrusions along the track, forming hemispherical sidewall protrusions; subsequent layer powder flows into these features, producing uneven layer thickness and affecting subsequent layer geometry</cite>. 
- Overlap and scan strategy control whether overhangs require support or can be self-supporting; insufficient overlap yields gaps and porosity, while excessive overlap increases crown and reduces build efficiency. <cite id="fc17a94e-0">Overlap between passes is a key geometry driver, with insufficient overlap risking gaps and porosity; DoE and process mapping are used to set overlap with power/speed/feed to ensure continuous clad geometry</cite>. <cite id="c53cfda6-4">A DED strategy study for Inconel 718 shows varying bead overlap alters bead geometry and surface roughness; mismatched contour–infill interactions increase porosity, so deposition strategy must coordinate contour curve spacing with infill pattern to maintain geometry integrity</cite>. 
- Nozzle/defocus and standoff also set vertical geometry and bridging stability. <cite id="85e47abf-3">At optimal standoff, clad height increases due to focused powder capture into the melt pool, while excessive standoff reduces height and penetration; this directly influences the vertical clearance and bridging geometry between passes</cite>.

6) Dimensional Fidelity: Strategy, Substrate Temperature, and Interpass Heat
- Dimensional accuracy emerges from consistent layer height and track width, governed by stable process windows and toolpath planning. <cite id="85e47abf-4">Experiments show that controlling laser power, feed rate, powder mass flow, and substrate temperature enables prediction and control of bead height, width, and contact angle; maintaining these variables reduces dimensional inaccuracies and poor bonding</cite>. 
- Substrate and interpass heat affect solidification and geometry fidelity; preheating or thermal management can stabilize geometry across layers. <cite id="85e47abf-4">A dedicated thermal conditioning setup with DoE confirmed that bead geometry metrics (height, width, contact angle) are sensitive to substrate temperature; regression models improved prediction across temperatures, supporting preheat-guided geometry control</cite>. 
- Scan strategy and path planning influence feature fidelity, especially for thin walls and variable cross-sections. <cite id="fc17a94e-1">Thin-wall Inconel 738 required low scanning speeds to avoid cracking and maintain geometry integrity; more generally, scan strategy and parameter tuning are intertwined to preserve feature geometry under high energy density</cite>. <cite id="c53cfda6-3">For SAM of Inconel 718, inter-track accumulation and uneven layer thickness along scan direction led to surface height differences that propagate to subsequent layers, degrading dimensional consistency across layers</cite>.

7) Practical Parameter Effects and Trade-offs for Nickel-Based Alloys
- Power–speed pairing to hit target cross-section: <cite id="fc17a94e-0">Travel speed of 5–20 mm/s and laser power in multi-kW regimes are typical; layer heights of 0.5–2 mm are targeted via feed tuning and overlap</cite>. <cite id="fc17a94e-3">Power is primary for width and deposition rate; speed modifies residence time and flow, affecting lateral spreading and crown formation</cite>. <cite id="85e47abf-3">Standoff/defocus reshape spot/powder fields; mapping these to clad width/height/penetration enables robust geometry</cite>. 
- Feed tuning and overlap to avoid gaps/balling: <cite id="fc17a94e-0">Adjusting feed rate for 0.5–2 mm layer heights and setting sufficient overlap prevents inter-track gaps and porosity; process maps tie these settings to consistent clad width and low porosity</cite>. <cite id="c53cfda6-4">Bead overlap changes bead geometry and surface roughness; strategy design that coordinates contour–infill reduces porosity and supports geometry fidelity</cite>. 
- Standoff and nozzle choice for vertical and inclined builds: <cite id="85e47abf-3">Optimized standoff can maximize clad height by focusing powder into the melt pool; too high or too low standoff reduces height and increases width due to inefficient catchment and spot-size effects</cite>. <cite id="85e47abf-2">Coaxial nozzles lose efficiency on inclined geometries; alternative nozzle geometries (discrete coaxial, powder-beam) improve catchment and bead geometry at high rates</cite>. 
- Thermal management for dimensional stability: <cite id="85e47abf-4">Substrate temperature is a first-order variable for bead geometry; regression models across temperatures show improved predictability of height/width/contact angle, guiding preheating strategies to stabilize geometry</cite>. 
- Alloy-specific thermal/phase effects: <cite id="c53cfda6-2">Inconel 718’s larger melt pools than Inconel 625 at similar parameters necessitate parameter offsets when porting builds; process windows must be alloy-tailored</cite>. <cite id="fc17a94e-1">Nickel-based alloys with γ′ phases are crack sensitive; low-speed/high-energy-density strategies used for thin walls also reduce geometry defects like keyholing/balling that distort cross-sections</cite>.

8) Modeling and DoE: Predicting and Controlling Geometry
- Physics-based and empirical models connect parameters to geometry to reduce trial-and-error. <cite id="fc17a94e-3">A 3D model coupling heat transfer, phase change, and flow for NiTi DED accurately predicted cladding geometry, melt pool depth, and deposition rate; power dominated width and deposition rate, while speed/feed affected geometry less in the tested ranges</cite>. <cite id="fc17a94e-2">For a nickel-based HEA, optimal 900 W/500 mm/min yielded distinct interfacial microstructures; beyond the first layer, dilution-driven geometry changes stabilized, supporting models that focus on initial-layer parameter sensitivity</cite>. 
- DoE and regression enable inverse design for target geometry: <cite id="85e47abf-4">Design of Experiments with substrate thermal conditioning produced linear/quadratic models mapping laser power, feed rate, powder mass flow, and temperature to bead height, width, and contact angle, validated experimentally for robust geometry prediction</cite>. <cite id="fc17a94e-0">Process mapping and DoE are standard to connect power–speed–feed–overlap to clad width consistency, porosity, and dilution, reducing geometry defects</cite>.

9) Summary: Parameter-to-Geometry Map for Nickel-Based Alloy DED
- Laser power: primary lever for clad width, penetration depth, and deposition rate; increases width/depth/height at a given speed via higher energy density, but raises risk of balling/porosity outside the stable window. <cite id="fc17a94e-3">Power is critical to melt pool width and deposition rate</cite> <cite id="85e47abf-2">studies identify power/speed as dominant geometry drivers</cite>. 
- Travel speed: inversely tunes energy density per unit length; lower speeds broaden and deepen pools, improve fusion but add heat-affected zones; used to suppress cracking and stabilize thin walls. <cite id="fc17a94e-1">Low speeds (high energy density) enable crack-free thin walls</cite> <cite id="c53cfda6-2">lower speeds yield larger melt pools</cite>. 
- Powder feed rate: sets cross-sectional area per track and interacts with speed and standoff; too high feed at fixed power/standoff creates sagging crowns and gaps; too low yields thin, porous layers. <cite id="fc17a94e-0">Feed rate tuned for 0.5–2 mm layers with adequate overlap</cite> <cite id="85e47abf-4">models link feed to bead height/width/contact angle</cite>. 
- Standoff and defocus: reshape the laser spot/powder envelope; narrow/optimized standoff increases clad height via focused powder capture; excessive standoff/defocus broaden width and reduce height and penetration. <cite id="85e47abf-3">Standoff/defocus map to clad width/height/penetration via altered catchment and spot size</cite>. 
- Scan strategy and overlap: determine inter-track continuity and overhang geometry; insufficient overlap causes gaps/porosity; excessive overlap increases crown and reduces efficiency. <cite id="fc17a94e-0">Overlap governs continuity and porosity</cite> <cite id="c53cfda6-4">overlap changes bead geometry/roughness; strategy design reduces porosity</cite>. 
- Substrate temperature and interpass heat: stabilize or destabilize geometry depending on thermal transport; preheating can improve predictability of bead height/width/contact angle across layers. <cite id="85e47abf-4">Substrate temperature significantly affects bead geometry metrics with controllable models</cite>. 
- Alloy chemistry: shifts thermal property baseline, altering melt pool size and geometry at fixed parameters; process windows must be alloy-specific. <cite id="c53cfda6-2">Inconel 718 shows larger pools than Inconel 625 at similar parameters</cite> <cite id="fc17a94e-1">nickel-based alloys are crack sensitive; parameter tuning stabilizes geometry</cite>.

Together, these findings provide a practical, evidence-backed framework: use power–speed maps to target desired clad width/penetration at alloy-appropriate energy density; set feed and overlap to achieve target layer height and continuous interfacial geometry; tune standoff/defocus and nozzle configuration for vertical and inclined builds; and apply substrate temperature and scan strategy to control crowns/bridges, surface roughness, and dimensional fidelity. <cite id="fc17a94e-0">Design-of-experiments and process mapping are recommended to translate these parameter–geometry relationships into robust build strategies</cite>.

Snippet: Abstract. Directed energy deposition (DED) is an additive manufacturing process which is increasingly being used for direct manufacturing, added function application and component repair of high-value metals and alloys that are otherwise hard to machine conventionally [1]. However, most commercially available toolpath generators are not comprehensive with regards to the deposition strategy and process parameters, emphasis usually being placed solely on the overlap of adjacent weld beads rather than including the interaction between the contour curves and infill pattern. This increases the probability of gap formation in the deposition pattern, and hence the rate of porosity in the part. This study focuses on the influence of varying bead overlap on the resulting bead geometry and surface roughness for Inconel 718 workpieces deposited using the DED process. The deposition strategy was devised using Python programming language, and the code found to be robust for both single- and multi-layer deposits.

Snippet: Directed Energy Deposition (DED) is a typical AM process for metal alloys that uses focused thermal energy, typically from a high-powered laser, to fuse materials by melting them as they are deposited (Bandyopadhyay and Heer 2018;De-bRoy et al. 2018). DED involves feeding metal in the form of powder or wire directly into the path of the energy source.

The process is conducted in an inert argon environment with oxygen levels typically below 20 ppm. Title: Numerical Simulation of Stainless Steel Powder Feeding in a Coaxial Nozzle for High Powder Efficiency in Laser Direct Energy Deposition
Snippet: Direct energy deposition (DED) is also called as laser engineered net shaping, direct metal deposition, and 3D laser cladding. This process is generally used to repair or add additional material to the existing component (Graf et al., 2012). The advantages of DED attract various metal part applications in aerospace, automobile, naval, and medical sectors, such as products of jet engines, turbines blades, or implant applications (Schmidt et al., 2017). DED is the most suitable approach to produce a large-scale freeform fabrication due to its high efficiency and the fact that it does not require any strict shielding system. This process has the ability to manufacture a heterogeneous material system with preferred properties and features via successive and concurrent depositions of different materials. In addition, a hybrid process combining DED with different manufacturing processes can be conveniently developed. Hence, research on the DED processes has been progressively increased in recent years. Furthermore, this method is used to repair damaged components, to manufacture new parts, and to apply wear and corrosion resistance coatings (Herderick, 2011). In DED, there are four types of powder feed mechanisms, such as off-axis powder injection, continuous coaxial nozzle, discrete coaxial nozzle, and inside powder-beam injection (Singh et al., 2020). This nozzle gives a higher efficiency only in the case vertical configurations but does not when the part is at an inclined angle due to its negative gravitational effect. This effect can be overcome by another type nozzle called discrete coaxial nozzle. In a powder-beam injection nozzle, the laser beam is divided and projected radially, concentrating at a point, and the powder is fed from the center of the nozzle. Manjaiah et al. (2020) studied the effect of DED process parameters on bead geometry at high-deposition-rate 316L SS powder using a coaxial nozzle. Most DED systems use a coaxial nozzle system in deposition head. It was concluded that the bead geometry was highly affected by scan speed and laser power. Zhong et al. (2015a) experimentally evaluated the effect of process parameters on porosity, bead geometry, deposition rate, and powder efficiency in a DED system using coaxial nozzle.

Title: Influence of standoff distance and laser defocusing distance on direct laser metal deposition of a nickel-based superalloy
Snippet: In this work, a series of experimental tests was carried out by using the direct laser metal deposition (DLMD) process. Nickel-based superalloy powders are convoyed through a coaxial nozzle on AISI 304 stainless steel plates. The effects of laser defocusing distance (F) and standoff distance (H) variations on the geometrical characteristics of the single deposited clad, in terms of clad width, clad height, penetration depth, and dilution, were analyzed. The following conclusions, under the tested conditions, were drawn: 

• An accurate analysis of the influence of standoff distance and defocusing distance on the laser beam profile and powder distribution was carried out. Correlated to the proposed analytical model, the analysis allowed the study of operating conditions with different process setups and correlate them with the geometrical characteristics of the clad. 

• An experimental setup was designed to evaluate the spatial distribution of powder. By means of a coaxial light beam and a laterally positioned camera, it was possible to define the powder distribution in different deposition planes identified by the experimental plan. The cumulative relative brightness (CRB) and envelope function have been proposed to relate the powder flow analysis with the geometrical characteristics of the clad. • The relationship between laser defocusing distance, standoff distance, and clad width was studied through an analytical model and experimental measurements. The results of both the experimental tests and the model revealed that an increase of the clad width was obtained as the laser spot size on the deposition plane increased. The effect of standoff distance is more complex to explain and is traced back to the powder distribution that interacts with the laser beam. • The variation of the standoff distance led to different heights of the deposited clad. A minimal clad height was detected for lower standoff distances when the powder flow concentrate on the border of the region of interaction with the laser beam. It increases in the standard deposition plane, when the powder focalized in the center of the melt pool, maximizing the powders catchment efficiency. By further increasing of the standoff distance, the clad height reduced again. On the other hand, the laser defocusing distance had a very little influence on the clad height. • The penetration depth decreased both with the increase of the laser defocusing distance and the standoff distance.

Title: Effect of Substrate Temperature on Bead Track Geometry of 316L in Directed Energy Deposition: Investigation and Regression Modeling
Snippet: The optimization of process parameters in powder Directed Energy Deposition (DED) is essential for achieving consistent, high-quality bead geometries, which directly influence the performance and structural integrity of fabricated components. As a subset of additive manufacturing (AM), the DED process, also referred to as laser metal deposition (LMD), enables precise, layer-by-layer material deposition, making it highly suitable for complex geometries and part repair applications. Critical parameters, such as the laser power, feed rate, powder mass flow, and substrate temperature govern the deposition process, impacting the bead height, width, contact angle, and dilution. Inconsistent control over these variables can lead to defects, such as poor bonding, dimensional inaccuracies, and material weaknesses, ultimately compromising the final product. This paper investigates the effects of various process parameters, specifically the substrate temperature, on bead track geometry in DED processes for stainless steel (1.4404). A specialized experimental setup, integrated within a DED machine, facilitates the controlled thermal conditioning of sample sheets. Using Design of Experiments (DoE) methods, individual bead marks are generated and analyzed to assess geometric characteristics. Regression models, including both linear and quadratic approaches, are constructed to predict machine parameters for achieving the desired bead geometry at different substrate temperatures. Validation experiments confirm the accuracy and reliability of the models, particularly in predicting the bead height, bead width, and contact angle across a broad range of substrate temperatures. However, the models demonstrated limitations in accurately predicting dilution, indicating the need for further refinement. Despite some deviations in measured values, successful fabrication is achieved, demonstrating robust bonding between the bead and substrate. The developed models offer insights into optimizing DED process parameters to achieve desired bead characteristics, advancing the precision and reliability of additive manufacturing technology. Future work will focus on refining the regression models to improve predictions, particularly for dilution, and further investigate non-linear interactions between process variables.

Below is an evidence-backed synthesis of how key process parameters in directed energy deposition (DED) of nickel-based alloys govern deposit geometry, including layer cross-section (width/height/penetration), surface and crown/bridge morphology, and dimensional fidelity. Mechanisms and quantitative trends are highlighted, with alloy-specific notes for nickel-based superalloys such as Inconel 625/718.

1) How DED Forms Deposit Geometry and Why Parameters Matter
- In powder-feed DED, a moving heat source (laser or electron beam) simultaneously melts fed powder and bonds molten material to the substrate and prior layers; geometry emerges from the melt pool’s heat, flow, and solidification under constraints set by toolpath, standoff, and nozzle physics. <cite id="fc17a94e-0">Key controllable inputs include laser/e-beam power, travel speed, powder feed rate, standoff distance, and pass overlap; these directly set clad width, height, penetration depth, dilution, and thus part geometry and microstructural homogeneity</cite>. 
- Alloy chemistry modulates the thermal-transport window; even within “nickel-based,” thermal properties differ enough to shift melt pool dimensions for comparable parameters. <cite id="c53cfda6-2">Inconel 718 shows larger melt pool dimensions than Inconel 625 under similar conditions due to differences in thermal properties, underscoring the need to co-optimize process parameters with alloy-specific thermal behavior</cite>.

2) Power, Speed, and Energy Density: Width, Penetration, and Height
- Laser power is typically the dominant driver of lateral and volumetric geometry: higher power enlarges the melt pool footprint and increases deposition rate, which enlarges clad width and depth and raises material catchment per track. <cite id="fc17a94e-3">In DED of NiTi, laser power critically determines melt pool width and deposition rate; scan speed and feed rate had comparatively smaller effects on cladding geometry across tested ranges, with fluid velocity controlling elemental redistribution within the pool</cite>. <cite id="85e47abf-2">Analytical and experimental studies with coaxial nozzles conclude bead geometry is highly affected by scan speed and laser power, with process maps tying porosity, bead geometry, deposition rate, and powder efficiency to power–speed settings</cite>. 
- Travel speed sets energy density per unit area and time; lowering speed at fixed power increases heat input, deepens penetration, and broadens width, but risks interlayer balling and thermal stress. <cite id="fc17a94e-1">For thin-walled Inconel 738, crack-free deposition was achieved using low scanning speeds to induce high energy density, illustrating how higher energy density enlarges molten pools and stabilizes melting in crack-sensitive nickel-based alloys</cite>. <cite id="c53cfda6-2">Across Inconel 625 and 718, numerical melt pool simulations show material thermal properties govern depth/width; higher effective energy density (low speed/high power) enlarges pools, and alloy differences produce distinct geometry responses at identical parameters</cite>.
- Interaction maps are essential to avoid geometry defects: <cite id="fc17a94e-0">process maps linking power–speed interactions to clad width consistency and porosity below 1% are used to define stable windows; outside these windows, molten pool instability (e.g., balling) degrades geometry and homogeneity</cite>. <cite id="fc17a94e-3">Modeling/experiment correlation shows power governs cladding width and deposition rate, while speed alters residence time and fluid flow, changing cross-section and element distribution</cite>.

3) Powder Feed Rate and Nozzle/Standoff Geometry
- Feed rate sets cross-sectional area per track; it interacts with speed and pool depth to set bead height and surface continuity. <cite id="fc17a94e-0">Industrial DED practice tunes feed rate to target layer heights of 0.5–2 mm, with overlap chosen to fill inter-track gaps and achieve desired cross-section</cite>. <cite id="85e47abf-4">Regression models for bead geometry show bead height, width, and contact angle are functions of laser power, feed rate, powder mass flow, and substrate temperature, enabling prediction of parameters to hit target geometry</cite>. 
- Standoff distance (nozzle-to-workpiece) and laser defocus reshape the beam spot and powder catchment, strongly affecting clad height and width. <cite id="85e47abf-3">For a nickel-based superalloy with a coaxial nozzle, increasing standoff distance first reduces clad width via spot-size and powder distribution changes, then increases clad height at an optimum standoff where powder focuses on the melt pool center, before decreasing height again as powder spreads inefficiently; penetration depth decreases with increased standoff/defocus due to lower energy density and poorer convergence of powder into the pool</cite>. 
- Nozzle physics and powder delivery strategy matter at high rates or off-normal orientations. <cite id="85e47abf-2">Coaxial nozzles concentrate powder into the beam; their efficiency drops on inclined builds due to gravity-driven radial spreading, while discrete coaxial or powder-beam nozzles improve catchment; studies report bead geometry highly sensitive to power/speed in coaxial configurations</cite>. <cite id="85e47abf-2">Zhong et al. showed process parameters control porosity, bead geometry, and powder efficiency simultaneously, reinforcing the need to co-optimize feed, power, and speed for robust geometry</cite>.

4) Cross-Sectional Features: Width, Height, Contact Angle, Dilution, Penetration
- Clad width and height (layer thickness) are the primary descriptors of cross-section; contact angle and dilution quantify bonding and lateral mixing. <cite id="85e47abf-3">Experiments show clad width grows with spot size on the deposition plane; standoff/defocus shift powder distribution and thus width, height, and dilution</cite>. <cite id="85e47abf-4">Design-of-experiments on 1.4404 stainless steel yielded regression models predicting bead height, width, and contact angle from power, feed, powder mass flow, and substrate temperature; models were less reliable for dilution, indicating dilution is sensitive to transient pool behavior and interpass heat</cite>. 
- Penetration depth and dilution evolve with energy input and standoff: <cite id="85e47abf-3">higher energy density and focused powder delivery increase penetration; increasing standoff and defocus reduce spot concentration and lower penetration, while also altering clad height via powder catchment efficiency</cite>. <cite id="fc17a94e-2">In stable deposition beyond the first layer, uniform interfacial microstructures emerge, but dilution effects are strongest at the initial layers where substrate melting and mixing dominate geometry</cite>.
- Alloy-dependent thermal response shapes achievable cross-sections. <cite id="c53cfda6-2">Inconel 718 shows larger melt pools than Inconel 625 at similar parameters; this guides parameter offsets when transferring build geometries between nickel-based alloys</cite>. <cite id="fc17a94e-3">For NiTi, power-dominated width and deposition rate set the cross-section baseline even as speed/feed modulate flow and element distribution; this mechanism generalizes to nickel-based alloys where phase transformation and latent heat can alter pool dynamics</cite>.

5) Surface Morphology, Crown/Bridge Morphology, and Layer-by-Layer Geometry
- Crown height and bridge morphology arise from overlapping beads and molten material redistribution; they are sensitive to energy density, overlap, and standoff. <cite id="fc17a94e-3">High-speed photography of Inconel 718 DED shows accumulation of molten material at protrusions along the track, forming hemispherical sidewall protrusions; subsequent layer powder flows into these features, producing uneven layer thickness and affecting subsequent layer geometry</cite>. 
- Overlap and scan strategy control whether overhangs require support or can be self-supporting; insufficient overlap yields gaps and porosity, while excessive overlap increases crown and reduces build efficiency. <cite id="fc17a94e-0">Overlap between passes is a key geometry driver, with insufficient overlap risking gaps and porosity; DoE and process mapping are used to set overlap with power/speed/feed to ensure continuous clad geometry</cite>. <cite id="c53cfda6-4">A DED strategy study for Inconel 718 shows varying bead overlap alters bead geometry and surface roughness; mismatched contour–infill interactions increase porosity, so deposition strategy must coordinate contour curve spacing with infill pattern to maintain geometry integrity</cite>. 
- Nozzle/defocus and standoff also set vertical geometry and bridging stability. <cite id="85e47abf-3">At optimal standoff, clad height increases due to focused powder capture into the melt pool, while excessive standoff reduces height and penetration; this directly influences the vertical clearance and bridging geometry between passes</cite>.

6) Dimensional Fidelity: Strategy, Substrate Temperature, and Interpass Heat
- Dimensional accuracy emerges from consistent layer height and track width, governed by stable process windows and toolpath planning. <cite id="85e47abf-4">Experiments show that controlling laser power, feed rate, powder mass flow, and substrate temperature enables prediction and control of bead height, width, and contact angle; maintaining these variables reduces dimensional inaccuracies and poor bonding</cite>. 
- Substrate and interpass heat affect solidification and geometry fidelity; preheating or thermal management can stabilize geometry across layers. <cite id="85e47abf-4">A dedicated thermal conditioning setup with DoE confirmed that bead geometry metrics (height, width, contact angle) are sensitive to substrate temperature; regression models improved prediction across temperatures, supporting preheat-guided geometry control</cite>. 
- Scan strategy and path planning influence feature fidelity, especially for thin walls and variable cross-sections. <cite id="fc17a94e-1">Thin-wall Inconel 738 required low scanning speeds to avoid cracking and maintain geometry integrity; more generally, scan strategy and parameter tuning are intertwined to preserve feature geometry under high energy density</cite>. <cite id="c53cfda6-3">For SAM of Inconel 718, inter-track accumulation and uneven layer thickness along scan direction led to surface height differences that propagate to subsequent layers, degrading dimensional consistency across layers</cite>.

7) Practical Parameter Effects and Trade-offs for Nickel-Based Alloys
- Power–speed pairing to hit target cross-section: <cite id="fc17a94e-0">Travel speed of 5–20 mm/s and laser power in multi-kW regimes are typical; layer heights of 0.5–2 mm are targeted via feed tuning and overlap</cite>. <cite id="fc17a94e-3">Power is primary for width and deposition rate; speed modifies residence time and flow, affecting lateral spreading and crown formation</cite>. <cite id="85e47abf-3">Standoff/defocus reshape spot/powder fields; mapping these to clad width/height/penetration enables robust geometry</cite>. 
- Feed tuning and overlap to avoid gaps/balling: <cite id="fc17a94e-0">Adjusting feed rate for 0.5–2 mm layer heights and setting sufficient overlap prevents inter-track gaps and porosity; process maps tie these settings to consistent clad width and low porosity</cite>. <cite id="c53cfda6-4">Bead overlap changes bead geometry and surface roughness; strategy design that coordinates contour–infill reduces porosity and supports geometry fidelity</cite>. 
- Standoff and nozzle choice for vertical and inclined builds: <cite id="85e47abf-3">Optimized standoff can maximize clad height by focusing powder into the melt pool; too high or too low standoff reduces height and increases width due to inefficient catchment and spot-size effects</cite>. <cite id="85e47abf-2">Coaxial nozzles lose efficiency on inclined geometries; alternative nozzle geometries (discrete coaxial, powder-beam) improve catchment and bead geometry at high rates</cite>. 
- Thermal management for dimensional stability: <cite id="85e47abf-4">Substrate temperature is a first-order variable for bead geometry; regression models across temperatures show improved predictability of height/width/contact angle, guiding preheating strategies to stabilize geometry</cite>. 
- Alloy-specific thermal/phase effects: <cite id="c53cfda6-2">Inconel 718’s larger melt pools than Inconel 625 at similar parameters necessitate parameter offsets when porting builds; process windows must be alloy-tailored</cite>. <cite id="fc17a94e-1">Nickel-based alloys with γ′ phases are crack sensitive; low-speed/high-energy-density strategies used for thin walls also reduce geometry defects like keyholing/balling that distort cross-sections</cite>.

8) Modeling and DoE: Predicting and Controlling Geometry
- Physics-based and empirical models connect parameters to geometry to reduce trial-and-error. <cite id="fc17a94e-3">A 3D model coupling heat transfer, phase change, and flow for NiTi DED accurately predicted cladding geometry, melt pool depth, and deposition rate; power dominated width and deposition rate, while speed/feed affected geometry less in the tested ranges</cite>. <cite id="fc17a94e-2">For a nickel-based HEA, optimal 900 W/500 mm/min yielded distinct interfacial microstructures; beyond the first layer, dilution-driven geometry changes stabilized, supporting models that focus on initial-layer parameter sensitivity</cite>. 
- DoE and regression enable inverse design for target geometry: <cite id="85e47abf-4">Design of Experiments with substrate thermal conditioning produced linear/quadratic models mapping laser power, feed rate, powder mass flow, and temperature to bead height, width, and contact angle, validated experimentally for robust geometry prediction</cite>. <cite id="fc17a94e-0">Process mapping and DoE are standard to connect power–speed–feed–overlap to clad width consistency, porosity, and dilution, reducing geometry defects</cite>.

9) Summary: Parameter-to-Geometry Map for Nickel-Based Alloy DED
- Laser power: primary lever for clad width, penetration depth, and deposition rate; increases width/depth/height at a given speed via higher energy density, but raises risk of balling/porosity outside the stable window. <cite id="fc17a94e-3">Power is critical to melt pool width and deposition rate</cite> <cite id="85e47abf-2">studies identify power/speed as dominant geometry drivers</cite>. 
- Travel speed: inversely tunes energy density per unit length; lower speeds broaden and deepen pools, improve fusion but add heat-affected zones; used to suppress cracking and stabilize thin walls. <cite id="fc17a94e-1">Low speeds (high energy density) enable crack-free thin walls</cite> <cite id="c53cfda6-2">lower speeds yield larger melt pools</cite>. 
- Powder feed rate: sets cross-sectional area per track and interacts with speed and standoff; too high feed at fixed power/standoff creates sagging crowns and gaps; too low yields thin, porous layers. <cite id="fc17a94e-0">Feed rate tuned for 0.5–2 mm layers with adequate overlap</cite> <cite id="85e47abf-4">models link feed to bead height/width/contact angle</cite>. 
- Standoff and defocus: reshape the laser spot/powder envelope; narrow/optimized standoff increases clad height via focused powder capture; excessive standoff/defocus broaden width and reduce height and penetration. <cite id="85e47abf-3">Standoff/defocus map to clad width/height/penetration via altered catchment and spot size</cite>. 
- Scan strategy and overlap: determine inter-track continuity and overhang geometry; insufficient overlap causes gaps/porosity; excessive overlap increases crown and reduces efficiency. <cite id="fc17a94e-0">Overlap governs continuity and porosity</cite> <cite id="c53cfda6-4">overlap changes bead geometry/roughness; strategy design reduces porosity</cite>. 
- Substrate temperature and interpass heat: stabilize or destabilize geometry depending on thermal transport; preheating can improve predictability of bead height/width/contact angle across layers. <cite id="85e47abf-4">Substrate temperature significantly affects bead geometry metrics with controllable models</cite>. 
- Alloy chemistry: shifts thermal property baseline, altering melt pool size and geometry at fixed parameters; process windows must be alloy-specific. <cite id="c53cfda6-2">Inconel 718 shows larger pools than Inconel 625 at similar parameters</cite> <cite id="fc17a94e-1">nickel-based alloys are crack sensitive; parameter tuning stabilizes geometry</cite>.

Together, these findings provide a practical, evidence-backed framework: use power–speed maps to target desired clad width/penetration at alloy-appropriate energy density; set feed and overlap to achieve target layer height and continuous interfacial geometry; tune standoff/defocus and nozzle configuration for vertical and inclined builds; and apply substrate temperature and scan strategy to control crowns/bridges, surface roughness, and dimensional fidelity. <cite id="fc17a94e-0">Design-of-experiments and process mapping are recommended to translate these parameter–geometry relationships into robust build strategies</cite>. </answer>

Title: Cracking behaviour, microstructure evolution, and mechanical properties of GH4169/K477 by laser directed energy deposition
Snippet: Dual-nickel-based alloy blisks used in aeroengines are designed to meet the distinct requirements of the discs and blades [7]. The discs are typically made from high-ductility nickel-based alloys, while the blades are crafted from high-strength nickel-based alloys. Laser Directed Energy Deposition (LDED) is particularly wellsuited for manufacturing dual-alloy blisks, as it allows for the creation of a transition zone with graded powder ratios, facilitating the connection of dissimilar nickel-based alloys and mitigating differences in their physical and chemical properties [4,17]. However, the nickel-based alloys used for the blades, which often contain a relatively large amount of γ' phase, are highly crack-sensitive during LDED. Its mixtures with nickel-based alloys for discs are also crack-sensitive. This challenge must be addressed to achieve high-performance LDED of dual nickel-based alloy blisks. 

There are commonly two types of hot cracking in additive manufacturing (AM) of nickel-based alloys, i.e. solidification cracking and liquation cracking [37]. The addition and reduction of elements are accepted for hot cracking suppression. The addition of Hf and Y to Rene104 alleviated solidification cracking by reducing grain aspect ratios and improving melt pool fluidity [22]. The addition of Si suppressed solidification cracking in In939 by inhibiting primary dendrite arms growth [41], whereas reducing Si content was critical for crack suppression in In738 [43]. Removing the Hf element in CM247LC was shown to reduce hot cracking density by up to 75% [16], while further reducing Al content achieved crack-free AM by narrowing the freezing range and reducing low-melting-point phases at grain boundaries (GBs) [19]. It is noted that chemical composition adjustments are often costly, time-intensive, and not universally applicable, due to the complex cracking behaviour of nickel-based alloys. 

Process optimisation plays a critical role in crack suppression during AM. The crack-free deposition of thinwall In738 was achieved by employing low scanning speeds, which induced high energy density [32].

Title: Investigation of microstructural evolution at the melt pool interface in AlCoCrFeNi2.1 high-entropy alloy fabricated by laser-directed energy deposition
Snippet: To clarify the effect of melt pool dilution behavior on the microstructural evolution of high-entropy alloys during laser-directed energy deposition, this study investigates the deposition of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 on a 304L substrate. The optimal process parameters were determined as a laser power of P = 900 W and a scanning speed of v = 500 mm/min. Experimental results indicate that three distinct microstructures—planar crystals, columnar crystals, and eutectic structures—are present at the interface between the substrate and the deposited layer. The Fe element concentration decreases from the substrate to the eutectic region and stabilizes in the eutectic region at CFe = 16.3 %. The growth direction of the columnar crystals aligns with the temperature gradient in the melt pool, and Fe is primarily enriched within these columnar structures. During laser-directed energy deposition, the microstructural evolution within the melt pool mainly occurs in the initial deposition layer. In the subsequent stable deposition process, a uniform eutectic microstructure is consistently observed, demonstrating that the influence of dilution is primarily concentrated in the initial deposition stage.

Title: Molten pool characteristics of a nickel-titanium shape memory alloy for directed energy deposition
Snippet: Abstract Fabrication of nickel-titanium shape memory alloy through additive manufacturing has attracted increasing interest due to its advantages of flexible manufacturing capability, low-cost customization, and minimal defects. The process parameters in directed energy deposition (DED) have a crucial impact on its molten pool characteristics (geometry, microstructure, etc.), thus influencing the final properties of shape memory effect and pseudoelasticity. In this paper, a three-dimensional numerical model considering heat transfer, phase change, and fluid flow has been developed to simulate the cladding geometry, melt pool depth, and deposition rate. The experimental and simulated results indicated that laser power plays a critical role in determining the melt pool width and deposition rate while scan speed and powder feed rate have less effect on cladding geometry and deposition rate. The fluid velocity has a huge influence on the distribution of elements in the molten pool. The temperature gradient G, solidification rate R, as well as shape factor G/R were calculated to illustrate the underlying mechanisms of grain structure evolution. The grain morphology distribution of cross-section from the experimental samples agreed well with the simulation results. The model reported in this paper is expected to shed light on the optimization of the deposition process and grain structure prediction.

Dual-nickel-based alloy blisks used in aeroengines are designed to meet the distinct requirements of the discs and blades [7]. The discs are typically made from high-ductility nickel-based alloys, while the blades are crafted from high-strength nickel-based alloys. Laser Directed Energy Deposition (LDED) is particularly wellsuited for manufacturing dual-alloy blisks, as it allows for the creation of a transition zone with graded powder ratios, facilitating the connection of dissimilar nickel-based alloys and mitigating differences in their physical and chemical properties [4,17]. However, the nickel-based alloys used for the blades, which often contain a relatively large amount of γ' phase, are highly crack-sensitive during LDED. Its mixtures with nickel-based alloys for discs are also crack-sensitive. This challenge must be addressed to achieve high-performance LDED of dual nickel-based alloy blisks. 

There are commonly two types of hot cracking in additive manufacturing (AM) of nickel-based alloys, i.e. solidification cracking and liquation cracking [37]. The addition and reduction of elements are accepted for hot cracking suppression. The addition of Hf and Y to Rene104 alleviated solidification cracking by reducing grain aspect ratios and improving melt pool fluidity [22]. The addition of Si suppressed solidification cracking in In939 by inhibiting primary dendrite arms growth [41], whereas reducing Si content was critical for crack suppression in In738 [43]. Removing the Hf element in CM247LC was shown to reduce hot cracking density by up to 75% [16], while further reducing Al content achieved crack-free AM by narrowing the freezing range and reducing low-melting-point phases at grain boundaries (GBs) [19]. It is noted that chemical composition adjustments are often costly, time-intensive, and not universally applicable, due to the complex cracking behaviour of nickel-based alloys. 

Process optimisation plays a critical role in crack suppression during AM. The crack-free deposition of thinwall In738 was achieved by employing low scanning speeds, which induced high energy density [32].

snippet.text: To clarify the effect of melt pool dilution behavior on the microstructural evolution of high-entropy alloys during laser-directed energy deposition, this study investigates the deposition of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 on a 304L substrate. The optimal process parameters were determined as a laser power of P = 900 W and a scanning speed of v = 500 mm/min. Experimental results indicate that three distinct microstructures—planar crystals, columnar crystals, and eutectic structures—are present at the interface between the substrate and the deposited layer. The Fe element concentration decreases from the substrate to the eutectic region and stabilizes in the eutectic region at CFe = 16.3 %. The growth direction of the columnar crystals aligns with the temperature gradient in the melt pool, and Fe is primarily enriched within these columnar structures. During laser-directed energy deposition, the microstructural evolution within the melt pool mainly occurs in the initial deposition layer. In the subsequent stable deposition process, a uniform eutectic microstructure is consistently observed, demonstrating that the influence of dilution is primarily concentrated in the initial deposition stage.

Title: Influence of deposition strategy on porosity in powder-feed directed energy deposition (DED)
Snippet: Abstract. Directed energy deposition (DED) is an additive manufacturing process which is increasingly being used for direct manufacturing, added function application and component repair of high-value metals and alloys that are otherwise hard to machine conventionally [1]. However, most commercially available toolpath generators are not comprehensive with regards to the deposition strategy and process parameters, emphasis usually being placed solely on the overlap of adjacent weld beads rather than including the interaction between the contour curves and infill pattern. This increases the probability of gap formation in the deposition pattern, and hence the rate of porosity in the part. This study focuses on the influence of varying bead overlap on the resulting bead geometry and surface roughness for Inconel 718 workpieces deposited using the DED process. The deposition strategy was devised using Python programming language, and the code found to be robust for both single- and multi-layer deposits.

snippet.text: In laser-directed energy deposition (DED), the geometric characteristics of individual deposited layers—height (H) and width (W)—fundamentally determine the dimensional accuracy of final components. This study quantifies the effects of three key process parameters—laser power, scanning speed, and powder feed rate—on H and W to establish a quantitative basis for dimensional control. A full factorial design (5×4×3) was employed, generating 60 single-track samples. Three-way ANOVA was applied to identify significant factors, quantify contribution ratios, and examine interactions. Results show excellent model fit (H: R²=96.47%, W: R²=97.51%). For height H, powder feed rate dominates (57% contribution), followed by scanning speed (31%), while laser power shows no significant effect (P>0.05). For width W, laser power dominates (60%), followed by scanning speed (28%). A significant interaction exists between scanning speed and powder feed rate for width (P<0.001): at low speeds (<11.5 mm/s), increasing feed rate increases W; at high speeds (>11.5 mm/s), the opposite occurs. These findings reveal distinct parameter dominances—feed rate controls height, power controls width—providing a quantitative foundation for targeted parameter optimization in DED processes.

Title: Integrated Assessment of Mechanical and Electrochemical Properties of Additively Manufactured IN 718 Alloy Using Taguchi and Super Ranking Approaches
Snippet: The above literature review confirms that Inconel 718 exhibits a unique combination of compositional versatility, mechanical performance, and broad industrial applicability, encouraging further study to optimize parameters that enhance its material performance. 

In recent years, the impact of selective laser melting (SLM) variables (laser power, scan speed, argon or nitrogen conditions, build direction, and heat treatments) on microstructure (grain and precipitate morphology) and mechanical properties (strengths and hardness) of Inconel 718 parts was investigated [28]. The hot-isostatic pressing and build orientation showed a profound impact on mechanical properties, whereas atmospheric conditions had little influence. The scanning speed, laser power, hatch spacing, and scanning strategy on Inconel 718 were examined without formal optimization [29]. Scanning speed and strategy significantly impact density and mechanical strengths, as defects such as pores and cracks are minimized, resulting in a refined microstructure and high density. The impact of SLM variables such as laser power, scan speed, spot size, and volumetric energy density on mechanical performance (strength and hardness) and surface finish of Inconel 718 parts was investigated [30]. The regression models developed helped industry personnel correlate SLM variables and printing quality performances. Inconel 718 processed via LPBF was optimized using Taguchi and PCA methods with laser power, scan speed, scanning pitch, and interlayer angle at 140 W, 800 mm/s, 70 μm pitch, and 45˚, resulting in the highest tensile strength [31]. Interlayer angle was the most influential factor (> 90% contribution), with higher energy density leading to more dendritic/cellular crystal formation. In direct laser metal deposition AM of Inconel 718, scanning speed (2.5-5.0 mm/s), powder feed rate (17.94-28.52 g/min), and scanning strategy (unidirectional/bidirectional) were optimized using ANOVA. Low scanning speed and high powder feed rate increased build dimensions, while stable walls were achieved at 2.5 mm/s, 28.52 g/min, and unidirectional scanning [32].

Title: High-density direct laser deposition (DLD) of CM247LC alloy: microstructure, porosity and cracks
Snippet: Nickel-based alloys are known as non-weldable materials due to their complex characteristics. Consequently, additive manufacturing of these alloys is particularly challenging. In this paper, the influence of process parameters on the porosity, crack formation and microstructure of additively manufactured CM247LC nickel-based alloy is analysed. The feasibility of the direct laser deposition (DLD) process to manufacture crack-free and low-porosity CM247LC samples is studied. CM247LC samples were built on Inconel 718 that has similar chemical composition, to form hybrid superalloy parts. It was shown that crack-free and high-density CM247LC samples can be obtained through DLD without significant substrate preheating for certain parameter combinations: laser power in the range of 800–1000 W and powder feed rates between 6 and 8 g/min. High-cost and complex preheating was avoided that was commonly reported as necessary to achieve similar densities. For hybrid parts, a large beam diameter and slow scan speeds were employed to achieve optimal conditions as it was evident from the achieved bonding between the Inconel 718 substrate and the deposited layers. It was observed that good bonding between the two materials can be obtained with laser power values between 800 and 1000 W, scanning speed higher than 300 mm/min and powder flow rates of 6–8 g/min.

Title: On Microstructure Evolution and Mechanical Behavior of Near Equiatomic Nickel Titanium (NiTi) Alloys Fabricated by Laser Deposition of Elemental Powders
Snippet: The present results reveal how sensitive the microstructure evolution and mechanical behavior of nickel titanium alloys are to the processing parameters of laser deposition. From the microstructure investigation, it was clear that changing the processing parameters affects the microstructure and the precipitates deposited. Reducing the laser power and scan speed increases the deposition of second-phase precipitates, as insufficient heat and time are available to melt them. Conversely, increasing the laser power while maintaining a constant scan speed reduces the precipitates. Additionally, decreasing the scan speed while keeping the laser power constant minimizes the occurrence of cracks. For the nanoindentation results, all specimens showed some recovery. However, specimen 6 had the highest recovery values and this is due to the higher amount of titanium deposited which improved the functional property. It was observed that reducing the scan speed resulted in decreased hardness, while lowering the laser power increased hardness. This behavior is attributed to the number of precipitates formed and the influence of laser power and scan speed on their formation.
